keyTakeaways: For Edinburgh Fringe teams, captions, surtitles, subtitles, projection mode, and mobile viewer delivery describe different decisions, not one interchangeable workflow.
A non-English show that mainly needs translation should usually specify prepared English surtitles for live performance, even if audience-facing copy says English subtitles.
Captions may need speaker identification, music, sound effects, off-stage audio, and other access information, not only translated dialogue.
projection mode and mobile viewer delivery are audience delivery choices; they should be chosen after the team defines whether the text is translation, captioning, or both.
Before tech rehearsal, Fringe teams should confirm text content, delivery method, language tracks, access requirements, and who owns live text operation.

faq.question: Does an Edinburgh Fringe show need captions or surtitles?
faq.answer: It depends on the audience need. A non-English show that needs translation for English-speaking audiences usually needs prepared English surtitles. A show with D/deaf or hard-of-hearing access requirements may need captions that include speaker labels, music, sound effects, and other audio information.

faq.question: Can we say English subtitles in our Fringe listing?
faq.answer: Yes. English subtitles is often clear audience-facing language. For production planning, prepared English surtitles is usually more precise when the text is a reviewed translation cued during a live show.

faq.question: What is the difference between surtitles and captions for Fringe productions?
faq.answer: Surtitles usually mean prepared translation text for a live performance in another language. Captions usually support access to speech and sound information, including dialogue, speaker identification, off-stage voices, music, or effects.

faq.question: Are projection mode and mobile viewer delivery the same as captions or surtitles?
faq.answer: No. projection mode and mobile viewer delivery describe how the audience receives the text. Captions and surtitles describe what kind of text is being prepared.

faq.question: What should a producer confirm before tech rehearsal?
faq.answer: Confirm whether the show needs English surtitles, captions, or both; which languages are enabled; whether projection, mobile viewer delivery, or both will be used; who reviews the text; and who operates or supervises live delivery.

faq.question: When is SurtitleLive a fit for a Fringe show?
faq.answer: SurtitleLive fits best when the team has a script or mostly stable performance text, can review the text before opening, and needs prepared text delivered by projection mode, mobile viewer, or both during a live show.

glossary.definition: Prepared English translation text shown or delivered during a live non-English performance.
Text that represents dialogue and relevant sound information, often used to support D/deaf or hard-of-hearing audiences.
A familiar audience-facing term for translated or transcribed text, often used casually even when the production workflow is live surtitling.
A projection display setup for theatre screens or projectors when the venue supports shared visible text.
A browser-based audience view opened by link or QR code so audience members can read enabled text on their own phones.
Caption information that tells the audience who is speaking, especially when the speaker may not be visually obvious.
Caption content that represents meaningful non-dialogue audio such as music, off-stage sound, effects, or silence.
The rehearsal period when the production tests venue setup, delivery method, text timing, and live operation before performance.
